title: Transfer-matrix / partition-function view of the ES certificate set
connection: The set of e-slices e ≡ −p (mod 4) with −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N} ↔ a 1-D statistical-mechanics chain whose 'spins' are the prime factors of N and whose Boltzmann weight is the indicator of the product landing in −1 mod e.
why: Positivity of a partition function (Z > 0) is exactly ES(p); stat-mech has tools (Lee–Yang zeros, cluster expansions) for proving positivity/non-vanishing that number theory does not routinely use.
first_step: Write Z_p(β) = Σ_e Σ_{ab|N} exp(−β·dist(ab⁻¹, −1 mod e)) and numerically locate its complex-β zeros for p ≤ 10⁵; check whether zeros avoid the real axis uniformly (Lee–Yang-type) and whether the pattern differs at odd squares.

title: Ising model on the modular-hyperbola graph of N
connection: The modular hyperbola xy ≡ −1 (mod e) restricted to divisors of N ↔ an Ising/Potts model whose ground-state energy is 0 iff the e-slice is non-empty.
why: Ground-state problems on frustrated graphs are where spin-glass theory produces sharp phase diagrams; ES asks for 'no frustration' at every p.
first_step: Build the graph (vertices = divisors of N, edges = pairs with ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 mod e) for a few hundred p, compute frustration index vs log p, look for a universal scaling law.

title: Random matrix statistics of the ES solution-count sequence f(p)
connection: f(p) (number of 4/p solutions) ↔ eigenvalue-count statistics; ask whether the normalized fluctuations of f(p)/log²p follow a known RMT law (GUE/GOE/Poisson) or a Selberg-class law.
why: If f(p) behaves like a 'spectral count' of some operator, then a lower bound f(p) ≥ 1 could be a spectral gap statement instead of a sieve statement.
first_step: Compute f(p) for primes up to 10⁷ (repo has data), fit the distribution of f(p)/E[f] and its two-point correlation along primes; compare to Poisson and to divisor-function moments (Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum arcsine law).

title: Arcsine law for divisors applied to 4Cp+1
connection: Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum: divisors of a typical n are arcsine-distributed on the log scale ↔ ES needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in a specific residue class −1 mod 4C, for SOME C.
why: Averaging over C (not over p) is a legitimate thick object at a fixed p; the arcsine law tells where divisors cluster, suggesting which C-range to aim at.
first_step: Search 'arcsine law divisors residue class' and check whether a residue-class-restricted DDT theorem exists (Tenenbaum's work on divisors in APs); then test numerically on 4Cp+1, C ≤ p, for fixed p.
refs: Deshouillers, Dress, Tenenbaum, Lois de répartition des diviseurs (1979)

title: Quantum-chaos / Berry–Tabor view of the e-slice as an integrable billiard
connection: The levels x = (quantity with p in it) of an integrable system have Poisson statistics (Berry–Tabor); the ES certificate x values for fixed p might be modelled by a 2-torus billiard's level set.
why: Poisson statistics would make f(p) ~ Poisson(log²p) with P(f=0) = exp(−c log²p), which is the heuristic ES already relies on; a rigorous Berry–Tabor-type theorem for a suitable flow would be a 'new input'.
first_step: Read Marklof's survey on Berry–Tabor for values of quadratic forms; check whether the e-slice set {(a,b): ab | N, ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 mod e} can be stated as values of a binary form at lattice points.

title: Integrable lattice model whose conserved quantity is 4/n − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z
connection: Discrete integrable maps (QRT maps, Painlevé discretizations) preserve rational invariants; ask whether U_n: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is the level set of a QRT-type invariant whose dynamics move integer points.
why: Markoff-type surfaces have Vieta involutions generating all integer points; U_n is a cubic surface too, and an integrable birational map might generate solutions from a seed.
first_step: Check whether U_n admits a non-trivial birational automorphism group of infinite order (compute via Magma/Sage: automorphisms of the cubic surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) preserving the integral structure); see if the Vieta-style 'flip in one variable' is well-defined for this equation.

title: Bethe-ansatz-like counting of ES solutions via a quantum many-body spectrum
connection: Solutions of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z ↔ Bethe roots of a 3-particle system where total 'momentum' 4/n is shared; completeness of Bethe ansatz = existence of a root configuration.
why: Completeness theorems for Bethe ansatz are existence statements proved for every n (e.g. XXX chain for all lengths), by algebraic rigidity — one of the two mechanisms (R) the campaign identified as able to give pointwise results.
first_step: Search 'Bethe ansatz Egyptian fractions' and 'Bethe equations unit fractions'; otherwise try to write the Bethe equations of a 3-magnon sector of a chain of length n and compare with the unit-fraction structure.

title: Kirchhoff/resistor networks: 4/n as equivalent resistance of three parallel resistors
connection: 1/x+1/y+1/z is the conductance of three parallel resistors; ES says a conductance 4/n is achievable with three integer resistors. Networks with series-parallel structure and integer values have been studied (Erdős-style problems on resistor networks).
why: Resistance of integer networks has nontrivial density results (Amengual, Khan: all rationals from unit resistors); a 'three-branch' restriction is the ES question and might inherit a trick.
first_step: Search 'integer resistors three parallel rational conductance' and 'Khan resistor network Egyptian fractions'; check whether any representation-theoretic argument (Farey/Stern–Brocot for series–parallel) gives three-term unit-fraction sums.
refs: S. A. Khan, 'Farey sequences and resistor networks' (Proc. Indian Acad. Sci. 2012)

title: Optics: thin-lens equation 1/f = 1/u + 1/v as Egyptian fractions
connection: Unit-fraction sums appear in lens/mirror equations; 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is three cascaded optical elements with integer focal lengths. Integer-focal-length lens combinatorics (Gaussian lens formula over ℤ) is a tiny literature.
why: Could supply a geometric (ray-transfer matrix, SL₂(ℤ)) model of unit-fraction sums that matches the known SL₂-word reformulation of ES.
first_step: Write the ray-transfer matrices of three thin lenses with focal lengths x,y,z in contact and compare with the SL₂ word form of ES (FRONTIER §1 'SL₂ words'); search 'integer focal lengths unit fractions'.

title: Sandpile/abelian-network identity element and divisors of 4Cp+1
connection: Chip-firing on the cycle graph ℤ/e with e ≡ −p mod 4 has a group structure (sandpile group ≅ ℤ/e); the e-slice condition −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹} is membership of −1 in a subset-product set inside this group.
why: Sandpile identities have surprising explicit structure (Levine–Propp); seen in repo as bsA_selling_sandpile but the specific 'subset-product set hits −1' angle may not be.
first_step: git grep sandpile in BRAINSTORM; then check whether the subset-product set {ab⁻¹ : ab | N} mod e is ever a subgroup or a coset (compute for p ≤ 10⁴).

title: Percolation threshold on the 'divisor-in-class' bipartite graph across C
connection: Build the bipartite graph with left vertices C ∈ [1,X], right vertices residue classes mod 4C, edge if 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C. ES(p) is 'some left vertex has its target edge'. Percolation thresholds as X grows ↔ how fast the first winning C appears.
why: The first winning C, C_min(p), is a natural 'order parameter'; its growth law (log p? p^ε?) is what any pointwise proof must beat.
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for all primes p ≤ 10⁷ (cheap), fit distribution; check whether the repo already has this (git grep 'C_min' or 'smallest C').

title: Renormalization-group flow on the Mordell residue classes mod 840·k
connection: Mordell's covering by identities reduces hard primes to 6 square classes mod 840; iterating to larger moduli (840·k) is an RG-like coarse-graining; the fixed point structure (what fraction of classes stay hard as modulus grows) is a computable 'critical exponent'.
why: Mordell–Schinzel says squares are never covered, but the *rate* at which non-square hard classes are absorbed by polynomial identities is a measurable quantity; a scaling law might suggest a non-polynomial identity family.
first_step: Compute, for moduli M = 840·k, k ≤ 50, the fraction of residues r mod M with r not covered by any known polynomial identity of degree ≤ 2; plot vs M; compare with density of non-squares.

title: Anderson localization analogy: ES certificate as an extended state
connection: The residue-class constraint f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) with f | p²+4c²d resembles a disordered 1-D hopping problem (random 'potential' from the factorization of p²+4c²d); a solution is a resonant state.
why: Localization theory proves existence of extended/localized states for *all* realizations via Furstenberg/Kotani (deterministic, not average), which is pointwise-in-disorder technology.
first_step: Define the transfer matrix M_c = product over prime factors of p²+4c²d of 2×2 matrices encoding the residue mod 4cd, and compute Lyapunov exponents; see if 'λ = 0 at some c' correlates with ES solutions.

title: Dyson's 'sphere-packing of unit fractions' metaphor: energy minimization over Egyptian fraction triples
connection: Treat (x,y,z) as particles with energy E = |4/n − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z|; ES is 'ground state energy is 0 for every n'. Energy-landscape methods (basin-hopping, simulated annealing) find ground states fast; the landscape's funnel structure might reveal a deterministic descent rule.
why: A deterministic descent that never gets stuck would be a proof; even failing that, the funnel geometry around the global minimum may suggest an invariant.
first_step: Run basin-hopping on E over (x,y,z) ∈ [1, n²]³ for 1000 primes; record the sequence of local minima visited and check whether they correspond to continued-fraction convergents of 4/n.

title: Thermodynamic formalism of the Gauss map restricted to length-3 continued fractions
connection: ES₅ ⟺ a certain rational has continued-fraction length λ ≤ 3. Thermodynamic formalism (Mayer transfer operator, Bowen's formula) controls the distribution of CF lengths over rationals with given denominator.
why: Hensley's theorem (Zaremba density) uses exactly this machinery; pointwise results for specific denominators are the analogue of what ES needs.
first_step: Read FRONTIER on ES₅ and write down exactly which rational r(p,·) must have λ ≤ 3; then check Hensley 'Continued fractions, Cantor sets, Hausdorff dimension' for any pointwise (not density) statement.

title: Horocycle-flow equidistribution and the modular hyperbola xy ≡ −1 (mod e)
connection: Points of the modular hyperbola equidistribute (Kloosterman sums / horocycle flow); ES needs a point on the hyperbola with x,y both dividing N (a thin subset).
why: Equidistribution of hyperbola points in *sparse* subsets via Ratner-style unipotent dynamics has produced pointwise theorems (e.g. Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak); maybe a dynamical formulation handles the divisor restriction.
first_step: Read Shparlinski's survey 'Modular hyperbolas' §'points with restricted coordinates'; check whether divisor-restricted hyperbola points are addressed anywhere.

title: Markoff-surface 'strong approximation' (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak) adapted to U_n
connection: BGS prove the Markoff graph mod p is connected (almost all p) via Vieta moves; the ES surface U_n has a Brauer group ℤ/2 and no BM obstruction. A Vieta-like group action on integer points of U_n would convert existence into 'orbit meets the integral points'.
why: Repo says no analogous action is known — but a *partial* action (e.g. from the 3 'swap' symmetries plus a cremona transformation of the cubic) may exist and nobody computed its orbits.
first_step: Compute the automorphism group of the affine cubic surface U_n over ℚ in Sage (or by hand: it's a 'Cayley-type' cubic with three A1 singularities?); list its elements and check which preserve integrality.
refs: Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, Markoff triples and strong approximation

title: Quantum unique ergodicity of theta functions and the 'theta quotient' form of ES
connection: Repo mentions a theta-quotient reformulation. QUE for theta functions (Marklof, Lindenstrauss) gives equidistribution of their values; positivity of a specific theta quotient at a specific point is a pointwise question.
why: Theta functions have exact functional equations (rigidity) — a candidate for mechanism (R).
first_step: git grep -il 'theta quotient' -- '*.md' to find the repo's statement; then check whether the quotient is a ratio of Jacobi forms whose Fourier coefficients have a sign-rigidity (e.g. Kronecker–Hurwitz class-number formula).

title: Entropy of the ES solution set as a function of p: 'thermodynamic limit' test
connection: Define S(p) = log f(p). Is S(p) ≈ 2 log log p + c with bounded fluctuations (like an extensive quantity) or heavy-tailed? Thermodynamic self-averaging would give concentration; concentration is the enemy of counterexamples.
why: If S(p) concentrates with sub-Gaussian tails around 2 log log p, counterexamples are 'large deviations' and a large-deviation principle could be a route to an unconditional bound at least for 'typical' primes in explicit sets.
first_step: Use the repo's f(p) data (p ≤ 10⁸) to fit the tails of S(p) − mean; compare with Erdős–Kac-type normal law for ω(4Cp+1).

title: Aharonov–Bohm phase / holonomy around the odd-square obstruction
connection: T1 says certificate lines are empty at odd squares for a reciprocity reason. A 'holonomy' interpretation: going around the square locus in the (p, C) parameter plane picks up a sign (Jacobi symbol). Mechanisms with nontrivial holonomy are forced to fail at squares — which is exactly what the barrier demands of any proof.
why: Reformulating T1 as a topological phase might guide the design of a mechanism that *provably* has the right failure mode at squares.
first_step: Write the Jacobi symbol (−C/p)-type sign that vanishes/flips at squares as a function on the parameter plane; check whether it is the Brauer class of Bright–Loughran evaluated at the fibre.

title: Pólya's 'random walk on divisors' and first-passage to the class −1 mod 4C
connection: Model the multiplicative group (ℤ/4C)^× as a Cayley graph generated by the prime factors of 4Cp+1; the subset-product set is the set reachable in ≤ ω steps; ES(p) asks that for some C the walk reaches −1.
why: Reachability in Cayley graphs with few generators is studied in expander/diameter theory (Babai conjecture, Helfgott); diameters of abelian Cayley graphs are explicit.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, compute for each C ≤ 100 the subgroup generated by prime factors of 4Cp+1 mod 4C and whether −1 lies in it; separate 'subgroup misses −1' from 'subgroup contains −1 but subset-product misses'.

title: KAM-type persistence: solutions of 4/n persist under small perturbation of n
connection: A solution for n yields solutions for multiples of n; conversely, do solutions 'persist' from n to n+1, n+2 via small rational moves (the way KAM tori persist)? ES across consecutive integers is a 'persistence' problem.
why: Elsholtz–Tao's identities for n ≡ 2,3 mod 4 are such persistence rules; a complete persistence rule along primes ≡ 1 mod 24 would be a proof; partial rules give covering systems (B1 — but we are breadth-first).
first_step: Compute, for consecutive primes p < q ≤ 10⁵, the minimal 'edit distance' between solution sets (e.g. number of solutions for q within Hamming distance 1 in (x,y,z)/scaled coordinates); look for structure.

title: Casimir / zeta-regularized interpretation of Σ 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n
connection: Unit-fraction sums as 'energies' of a vibrating system; zeta-regularized sums 'Σ 1/k' over a finite subset equal 4/n. Totally wild, but 'Casimir energies as Egyptian fractions' might exist in the physics literature.
why: Pure lead-check; cheap.
first_step: Web search 'Casimir energy Egyptian fraction' and 'unit fractions quantum field'; keep only if a nontrivial identity surfaces.

title: Coupling-from-the-past / exact sampling of ES solutions to detect non-uniformity
connection: Propp–Wilson exact sampling of a uniformly random solution of 4/p; the sampling chain's mixing time as a function of p is a measurable complexity of the solution set.
why: If exact sampling is easy (chain couples fast), solution sets are 'structured'; structure is what a proof can exploit.
first_step: Design a Markov chain on solutions (moves: change one of (c,d,f) parameters in the Type I form) and measure coupling time for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Scattering theory: 4/p as a resonance of the Eisenstein series at a cusp
connection: The Eisenstein series Fourier coefficients involve divisor sums σ_s(n); divisor-type counts restricted to residue classes appear in Eisenstein series for Γ₀(4C). The number of divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C is a coefficient of an Eisenstein series on Γ₁(4C).
why: Converts the tied-modulus divisor count into a modular-form coefficient; sign/positivity of such coefficients across the level is a studied question (for Eisenstein series, coefficients are explicit character sums).
first_step: Write d_{−1 mod 4C}(4Cp+1) as (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ̄(−1) Σ_{d|4Cp+1} χ(d) and see whether summing over C turns the inner twisted divisor sum into something with a known positive main term (repo's M_BM?).

title: Hyperbolic lattice-point counting in a 'thin' cone: ES as a Selberg-pretrace positivity
connection: ES's Type II condition ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 is a 'determinant = 1' condition on a 2×2 integer matrix [[f, 2c], [2cd, f′]]... (up to normalization); counting such matrices with congruence constraints is hyperbolic lattice point counting.
why: Lattice-point problems in SL₂(ℤ) have error terms via spectral theory; the campaign's B3 says the main term is only log²p, but spectral *positivity* (not counting) might still apply to a cleverly weighted sum.
first_step: Verify exact matrix form: find integers such that det [[f, α],[β, f′]] = 1 encodes ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 (α β = 4c²dp); then check whether the congruence f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd is a Γ₀/Γ₁-type condition.

title: Replica trick / cavity method for the probability that f(p) = 0
connection: Spin-glass cavity method computes P(no solution) for random CSPs exactly in the large-N limit; ES at prime p is a CSP with ~log p 'variables' (primes of 4Cp+1) per C.
why: Cavity predictions could give a sharper heuristic for exp(−c log² p) and identify the 'hard' structure (which C dominate).
first_step: Formulate the per-C CSP: variables ε_q ∈ {0,1} for primes q | 4Cp+1, constraint Π q^{ε_q} ≡ −1 mod 4C; count solutions by brute force vs cavity estimate for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Frenkel–Kontorova / devil's staircase of the 'best C' function
connection: C_min(p) (smallest C with a winning divisor) as a function of p may show a staircase structure with plateaus at values tied to Mordell classes; devil's staircases arise from mode-locking in circle maps.
why: Mode-locking = rational rotation numbers = continued fractions, which is already an ES reformulation (ES₅).
first_step: Plot C_min(p) against p for p ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁷; look for plateau structure and its relation to p mod 840.

title: Ehrenfest-style 'recurrence': ES solutions along the sequence p → p+24k as a Poincaré recurrence
connection: Fix a solution template (c,d,f) and ask for which k it still works for p+24k; the recurrence set is an AP-union (polynomial identity) or empty. The density of 'recurrence times' is a dynamical invariant.
why: Quantifies how much of ES is 'covered by local identities' vs genuinely new at each prime.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴ and each solution, compute the set of k ≤ 10³ for which the same (c,d) with the forced f works for p+24k; histogram.

title: Z₂ gauge theory on the prime-factor hypergraph of {4Cp+1}_C
connection: Each C gives a set of primes; a sign assignment (Legendre symbol (q/·)) on primes is a Z₂ gauge field; ES requires a 'Wilson loop' (product of symbols) to equal a target at some C. Gauge-invariant content = the frustration pattern.
why: Gauge-theoretic language can isolate what is invariant under rechoosing C; T1 (squares) is manifestly gauge-invariant.
first_step: Write the product of Legendre symbols Π (−p/q) over q | 4Cp+1 and relate to the divisor-class condition via reciprocity; check whether a known 'reciprocity sign' identity makes the product identically computable.

title: Dimer / Kasteleyn determinant count of e-slice solutions
connection: Solutions on an e-slice are pairs (a,b) with ab | N and ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 (mod e); this is a perfect-matching-like count in a bipartite graph (a's vs b's) and Kasteleyn's method computes matching counts as Pfaffians.
why: Pfaffian expressions give exact, sometimes positive formulas (e.g. Aztec diamond), unlike sieve bounds.
first_step: Construct the bipartite graph for a few N and check planarity (likely not), then check whether the count has a determinant formula anyway via the group structure (it's a convolution over (ℤ/e)^×).

title: Turbulence-style intermittency statistics for f(p)
connection: Multifractal/intermittent behaviour of f(p) across p (moments ⟨f^q⟩ scaling anomalously) would indicate heavy tails; the campaign only has means and almost-all results.
why: Moment scaling exponents distinguish 'log-normal' from 'Poisson' models of f(p); the lower tail (f = 0) is the whole question.
first_step: Compute ⟨f(p)^q⟩ for q = −2..4 over primes in dyadic ranges up to 10⁸ using repo data; fit scaling exponents.

title: Painlevé VI and cubic surfaces: U_n as a character variety
connection: Cubic surfaces xyz + x² + y² + z² + ax + by + cz + d = 0 (Fricke/character varieties) carry Painlevé VI dynamics and nonlinear monodromy. Check whether U_n (4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)) is birational to such a Fricke cubic.
why: Fricke cubics have infinite integral automorphism groups (Markoff-type); if U_n is one, the orbit structure of integer points is the whole story.
first_step: Attempt the explicit birational map: put x = n·X etc. and complete to a Fricke normal form; or run Sage to compute the Picard lattice and (−2)-curves of the projective closure of U_n (repo already knows its singularities? git grep 'Fricke').

title: Fluctuation theorem / Jarzynski: average over C of exponential weights gives pointwise-in-p identities
connection: Jarzynski's equality turns an average of exp(−W) into a free-energy difference exactly, for every realization of the system. Analogue: an *exact* identity Σ_C w(C)·(#divisors of 4Cp+1 in class) = known function of p would be a 'fluctuation theorem' for ES.
why: Exact identities for weighted divisor sums over C at fixed p do exist (they are class-number-type formulas: Σ_C d_χ(4Cp+1) relates to L-values); positivity then becomes an L-value statement.
first_step: Search for exact formulas: Σ_{C ≤ X} Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} χ_{4C}(d) in terms of class numbers (Hurwitz–Kronecker type); check FRONTIER §2 M_BM derivation for what identity is used.

title: Spectral gap of the 'ES Laplacian' on the forest reformulation
connection: Repo mentions a forest reformulation. Forests have Laplacians; Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem counts spanning forests as determinants. Ask whether f(p) (or an e-slice count) is a determinant/minor of a p-dependent Laplacian.
why: Determinant formulas are exact and sometimes provably nonzero by congruence/sign arguments.
first_step: git grep -il forest -- '*.md' to find the repo's reformulation; test whether the count equals a Laplacian minor for p ≤ 100.

title: Conformal-field-theory c=1 / Gaussian free field model of Dedekind sums tied to 4/p
connection: Dedekind sums s(a,c) satisfy reciprocity and are governed by continued fractions; continued-fraction length λ(p) ≤ 3 (ES₅) might be expressible through Dedekind-sum identities (Rademacher's 3-term reciprocity).
why: Rademacher's three-term Dedekind reciprocity is exactly a 'three-term' relation — a formal resemblance to three unit fractions worth 30 minutes.
first_step: Write the ES₅ rational, compute its Dedekind sum, and test numerically whether ES solutions correspond to triples (a,b,c) in Rademacher's identity s(a,b)+s(b,c)+s(c,a) = ... with a 1/12-type constant involving 4/p.
refs: Rademacher, 'Generalization of the reciprocity formula for Dedekind sums' (1954)

title: Topological-insulator-style 'bulk-boundary' invariant: Mordell classes as a bulk, squares as the boundary
connection: The 6 square classes mod 840 are the 'boundary' where polynomial identities fail; a ℤ/2 invariant (Brauer class) separates bulk from boundary. Bulk–boundary correspondence predicts protected 'edge states' — here, solutions that exist for a reason that only works away from squares.
why: Pure analogy, but it gives a design principle: look for mechanisms indexed by a ℤ/2-valued invariant that is nontrivial exactly on non-squares (e.g. a Jacobi symbol (p/m) that is +1 at squares).
first_step: List all ℤ/2 invariants of the form 'Jacobi symbol of p w.r.t. something determined by (C,d)' that are identically +1 when p is a square, and check which the known Type I/II identities use.

title: Kinetic theory: 'collisions' of unit fractions under the Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy map as a Boltzmann process
connection: The greedy algorithm 4/n → 4/n − 1/⌈n/4⌉ → … produces a 'cascade'. Treat denominators as energies and the greedy step as a collision rule; ES asks whether the cascade can be arranged to terminate in 3 steps.
why: Standard greedy gives ≤ 4 terms for 4/n; getting 3 is the whole problem, and the kinetic view asks which 'collision rule' (non-greedy choice) shortens cascades.
first_step: Enumerate, for p ≤ 10⁴, all 'first steps' 1/x with x ≤ 2⌈p/4⌉ that leave a 2-term remainder (i.e. remainder (4x−p)/(px) is a sum of two unit fractions); characterize winning x by p mod small moduli.

title: Two-unit-fraction remainder: ES as 'reduce to the solved two-term problem'
connection: a/b = 1/y + 1/z is completely understood: solvable iff b has a divisor pattern (a divisor d of b² ... with d ≡ −b mod a style). So ES(p) ⟺ ∃x: (4x−p)/(px) is a two-term Egyptian fraction, which is a divisor condition on p²x² ... concretely on (4x − p)-related integers.
why: This is the standard route to the divisor form, but phrasing it as 'the two-term problem with a free parameter x' invites tools from the two-term theory (e.g. counting representations of a/b by two unit fractions is a divisor-count of b² in classes).
first_step: Write the two-term criterion for (4x−p)/(px) explicitly and compare with the repo's Type I/II divisor form to confirm equivalence; then search literature on the two-term equation with varying numerator (Nagell? Rav?).
refs: Rav, 'On the representation of rational numbers as a sum of a fixed number of unit fractions' (1966)

title: Statistical mechanics of covering systems: 'temperature' at which Mordell-style covers fail
connection: Each polynomial identity covers an AP of primes; covering systems have a Hough-type threshold (minimum modulus bounded). Translate: a complete ES cover by identities with moduli ≤ M is impossible (Mordell–Schinzel), but a cover with density 1 − δ(M) is possible; δ(M) is a 'free energy'.
why: The rate δ(M) → 0 quantifies B1 precisely; a slow decay says identities are not the way, a fast decay says the residual set is tiny and maybe handleable differently.
first_step: Compute δ(M) = density of residues mod M not covered by identities of degree ≤ 2 with parameter modulus ≤ M, for M = 840, 1680, 2520, …; fit.
refs: Hough, 'Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems'

title: Schwinger–Dyson / loop equations for the generating function of f(n)
connection: Define F(s) = Σ f(n) n^{−s}. Elsholtz–Tao estimate partial sums; a functional equation or 'loop equation' for F (from the multiplicative structure of the Type I/II divisor conditions) might give analytic continuation and thus pointwise info via a Perron formula with explicit kernels.
why: Repo has anal_dirichlet_series.md; the free-lane twist is to look for an algebraic relation among F and its twists rather than estimates.
first_step: git grep -il 'dirichlet series' BRAINSTORM; then compute F(s) numerically for Re s > 1 and test whether F(s)/ζ(s)³ or F(s)/ζ(s)²L(s,χ₋₄) is 'nice' (bounded, Euler product).

title: Gravitational lensing time-delay identities and unit fractions
connection: Fermat's principle for multiple images gives sums of reciprocals of distances; integer-distance lensing configurations are an unexplored source of Egyptian fraction identities (pure lead-check).
why: Cheap search; probably nothing.
first_step: Web search 'reciprocal distances integer identities lens equation Egyptian'; drop if nothing.

title: Gibbs measure on (C, divisor) pairs and a 'free energy ≥ 0' inequality
connection: Weight each pair (C, d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C) by w = C^{−s}; the partition function Z_p(s) for s slightly > 1 converges and ES(p) ⟺ Z_p(s) > 0. Positivity could follow from an identity Z_p(s) = (explicit positive L-value product) + (error) if the error is < main term pointwise.
why: The campaign's M_BM is such a main term; the free-energy framing suggests choosing s to maximise main/error ratio, i.e. a 'temperature' optimisation not previously done.
first_step: Numerically compute Z_p(s) for s ∈ {1.01, 1.1, 1.5, 2} and p ≤ 10⁵; see whether the ratio Z_p(s)/E_C[Z] concentrates better for some s.

title: Hydrodynamic limit of Elsholtz–Tao's f(n) along short intervals
connection: Σ_{n∈[N,N+H]} f(n) for H = N^θ: short-interval averages (Matomäki–Radziwiłł technology) of multiplicative-like functions. f is not multiplicative, but its Type I count is a divisor-type sum.
why: Short-interval results for divisor-type functions are strong (every short interval of length N^{0.5+ε} has its expected count); pushing H down to log^A N along primes would be 'almost pointwise'.
first_step: Search 'divisor function short intervals every interval' (Ivić, Matomäki); check what H is attainable for d(n) restricted to residue classes and whether the Type I count fits.
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł, Multiplicative functions in short intervals

title: Chaotic scattering: resonances of 4/n − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z = 0 as a 3-body problem
connection: The equation is the condition for three particles with 'masses' x,y,z to have total 'reduced mass' n/4 — reduced-mass combination 1/μ = Σ 1/m_i. Integer reduced-mass problems may have been posed in recreational physics.
why: Pure lead-check.
first_step: Search 'reduced mass integer unit fractions problem'; drop if nothing.

title: Entanglement-entropy-style 'area law' for solution counts across Type I/Type II
connection: f_I(p) and f_II(p) are counted separately; their mutual information (over p) measures how independent the two mechanisms are. If nearly independent, P(f=0) ≈ P(f_I=0)·P(f_II=0), squaring the exponent in the heuristic.
why: A quantitative independence statement (even EVIDENCE) sharpens the target: proving only f_I ≥ 1 or only f_II ≥ 1 may be the better-defined problem.
first_step: From repo data, compute correlation of f_I(p), f_II(p) and of their indicator-of-zero across p ≤ 10⁸; compare conditional distributions.

title: Lyapunov-function approach: a potential Φ(x,y,z;n) that strictly decreases under an explicit integer move until a solution is reached
connection: Many existence proofs (e.g. Fermat descent, Vieta jumping, Zagier's one-sentence proof structure) are 'potential + move'. Design a potential on near-solutions of 4/n and a move that decreases it.
why: If a move with a monotone potential exists on a finite set, termination = existence. The known failure at squares must show up as the move being undefined there.
first_step: Take near-solutions (x,y,z) with |4/n − Σ 1/x_i| minimal and try candidate moves (replace z by the nearest integer making the sum exact, then rebalance); check empirically whether any simple rule reaches a solution for all p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Quantum computing: Shor-like period finding gives a divisor in a residue class?
connection: Shor's algorithm finds the order of a mod N; ES needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C. Quantum algorithms can find divisors in prescribed classes (by factoring fully), so ES solutions are findable in poly(log p) quantum time *if they exist* — trivially. Non-trivial: is there a quantum 'witness' structure (e.g. a hidden subgroup) that exists for every p?
why: Framing the existence as a hidden-subgroup problem might reveal an algebraic structure (subgroup!) which is what proofs need; low confidence.
first_step: Write the e-slice condition as 'the function g(a,b) = ab⁻¹ mod e on the divisor lattice has −1 in its image' and check whether the image is ever a coset of a subgroup (computation for N ≤ 10⁶).

title: Self-organized criticality: is the distribution of C_min(p) a power law?
connection: If C_min(p) (first winning C) has a power-law tail, the 'rare hard primes' are scale-free and adversarial search at 10¹⁸ would find larger C_min than seen; if exponential, pointwise proofs 'should' exist with C ≤ (log p)^A.
why: Directly calibrates the shape a proof must take (bounded C ⇒ covering, polylog C ⇒ sieve-like).
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁷ and fit tail; check repo (git grep 'C_min\|smallest c' DISPROOF_AVENUES.md STATUS.md).

title: Fisher-information / Cramér–Rao bound on how well p mod M predicts f(p)
connection: Treat f(p) as a signal and residues of p mod various M as features; the mutual information I(f(p); p mod M) measures how much of ES is 'local'. Mordell's classes are the M=840 case.
why: A rigorous statement 'f(p) is asymptotically independent of p mod M for all M' would be a theorem of equidistribution type; conversely strong dependence would point to new identities.
first_step: Compute I(f(p) ≥ k; p mod M) for M | 2⁵·3²·5·7·11·13 and p ≤ 10⁷; list the M with highest information per bit.

title: Coppersmith's method for small divisors in a residue class of 4Cp+1
connection: Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham: given N and a residue class r mod M with M ≥ N^{1/4}, one can find all divisors of N ≡ r mod M in polynomial time. ES needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C; here M = 4C and N ≈ 4Cp, so M ≈ N/p — far above N^{1/4} when C ≥ p^{1/3}.
why: This means the search for a Type-II-style certificate at fixed C is *algorithmically trivial* (lattice reduction) for large C — which says the hard part is purely existential, not computational, and makes the 'divisor in a class' lattice explicit (a 2-dim lattice whose short vectors are the certificates).
first_step: Write the Howgrave-Graham lattice for 'divisor of N in class r mod M' with N = 4Cp+1, M = 4C; identify the short vectors with (f, f′) of the Type II form; check whether the lattice's determinant structure explains the log²p count.

title: Factoring with hints (Rivest–Shamir, Maurer): ES as 'one divisor with 1/2 of the bits known'
connection: If a divisor f of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod 4C, then its low bits (mod 4C) are known; Maurer/Rivest–Shamir show factoring with half the bits known is polynomial. Conversely the *existence* of such a 'half-known' divisor for some C is ES.
why: The crypto literature's reverse question — for which N do such hint-structured divisors exist for a given hint modulus — may have been studied for key-generation (e.g. 'RSA keys with prescribed residue primes').
first_step: Search 'divisors in a prescribed residue class existence density Lenstra' (Lenstra 1984, 'Divisors in residue classes'): Lenstra bounds the NUMBER of divisors in a class by a constant when M > N^{1/3}; check what this says about ES's counting shape (at most O(1) certificates per large C).
refs: H. W. Lenstra Jr., 'Divisors in residue classes', Math. Comp. 42 (1984)

title: Lenstra's 'divisors in residue classes' upper bound vs ES's needed lower bound
connection: Lenstra (1984) proves: the number of divisors of N in a fixed class mod M with M > N^{1/3} is ≤ 11 (and the divisors are computable). ES needs ≥ 1 for some C ∈ [1, ∞) with N = 4Cp+1, M = 4C.
why: Lenstra's proof is via a 2-D lattice and continued fractions — exactly the ES₅ CF-length structure; understanding why his argument caps the count might show what forces the count to be ≥ 1 somewhere (or that it cannot).
first_step: Read Lenstra 1984 §2; map his lattice to the Type II pair (f, f′); determine whether ES₅ (λ ≤ 3) is Lenstra's condition for a specific convergent.

title: Approximate-GCD problem (van Dijk–Gentry–Halevi–Vaikuntanathan) and the Type I form
connection: Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd. Many samples p² + 4c²d (varying c,d) each near a multiple of an unknown f is the 'approximate GCD' setting from homomorphic encryption; its hardness/easiness results describe when such common divisors exist.
why: AGCD theory has precise density statements for when noisy multiples share a divisor; flipping to existence is an ES-like 'tied' question.
first_step: Write the Type I condition as p² ≡ −4c²d (mod f): a quadratic residuosity condition (−d is a square mod f up to units). Compare with the AGCD lattice attack (Cohn–Heninger 2011) to see whether it enumerates ES certificates.

title: SAT/SMT encoding of ES for a symbolic prime: unsat core as a proof template
connection: Encode '4/p has no solution with x,y,z < p² and p ≡ 1 mod 24' with p as a bit-vector of width w; for each w the solver returns UNSAT (if ES holds there). The UNSAT cores / DRAT proofs for w = 8, 10, 12, … might converge to a human-readable argument.
why: Heule's SAT-based proofs (Pythagorean triples, Schur 5) found structure humans missed; the per-width proof sequence is a cheap experiment nobody seems to have run for ES.
first_step: Write a CNF via bit-blasting of 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) with x ≤ y ≤ z < 2^{2w}, p < 2^w; run kissat/cadical for w ≤ 12 with proof logging; inspect core size growth.

title: Presburger/automatic-sequence test: is the set of (p, C_min(p)) k-automatic in any base?
connection: Automatic sequences and k-regular sequences are decidable by Walnut; if the first winning C (or Type I minimal c) were k-regular in p, Walnut could *prove* ES in that regime. Almost certainly not, but the negative result would be informative: it shows ES is 'non-automatic' which rules out all finite-automaton covering proofs.
why: Cheap and decisive one way or the other; connects to B1 in automaton language.
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁶, test for 2-/3-/10-regularity with a k-kernel rank test (compute subsequences C_min(k^e p + r) and check linear dependence).
refs: Shallit, 'The Logical Approach to Automatic Sequences' (Walnut)

title: Decidability frontier: ES as a Π₁ sentence of bounded-quantifier arithmetic — is it provable in IΔ₀ + exp?
connection: ES is Π₂ (∀n ∃x,y,z) but with the bound x,y,z ≤ n² (true for ES? solutions can be bounded by n² in Type II forms? check) it is Π₁ with bounded search. Reverse-mathematics / bounded-arithmetic questions: which fragment proves the known partial results (Mordell identities are in IΔ₀; Vaughan's sieve needs exp).
why: Proof-theoretic strength calibration tells what style of argument can possibly work: if ES is provable in IΔ₀+Ω₁ then there is a 'polynomial-size certificate' explanation, which constrains the proof shape.
first_step: Check whether there is always a solution with max(x,y,z) ≤ n² (compute for n ≤ 10⁵; known bounds for Type II give z ≤ ...). Then search 'Erdős–Straus bounded arithmetic' / 'unit fractions IΔ0'.

title: Kolmogorov complexity of the solution 'script' (c,d,f) across primes
connection: For each p, encode the lexicographically first Type I/II solution as a string; measure compressibility across consecutive primes (gzip of the concatenation, or a learned model's perplexity). Low complexity = hidden rule.
why: Direct test for 'there is a simple hidden rule the campaign has not found'. Cheap.
first_step: Produce the (c,d,f) first-solution sequence for p ≤ 10⁶, compress with xz/zpaq, compare with compressibility of a surrogate random sequence with the same marginals.

title: Program synthesis (enumerative/DreamCoder) for a 'solution formula' with branching on residues
connection: Search the space of programs 'if p ≡ r mod M then (x,y,z) = (polynomials in p)' with sqrt/floor allowed (non-polynomial! escaping Mordell–Schinzel) that output a valid ES solution on as many primes as possible.
why: Mordell–Schinzel kills polynomial identities on square classes; identities with floor, gcd, or ⌊√p⌋ are not covered by that theorem and nobody has systematically searched them.
first_step: Define a DSL: polynomials in p, ⌊√p⌋, ⌊p/k⌋, gcd(p+a, b), residue branching; run enumerative search (depth ≤ 6) scoring on primes ≡ 1 mod 840 up to 10⁵; report best coverage.
refs: Mordell–Schinzel (no polynomial identity on square classes)

title: Symbolic regression on f(p) to find a closed-form main term with explicit arithmetic corrections
connection: Fit f(p) ≈ A log²p + B log p · g(p) + ... where g ranges over arithmetic features (number of prime factors of p−1, p+1, class number h(−p), h(−4p), least QNR, Legendre symbols of small primes).
why: If a class-number or L-value feature explains a large part of the variance, it hints that f(p) is 'really' a class-number-type quantity (which would be an exact-formula route).
first_step: Build a feature table for primes ≤ 10⁶ (h(−4p), h(−p), ω(p±1), (2/p),(3/p),(5/p),(7/p), smallest prime factor of 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1 …); run PySR/LASSO on f(p)/log²p; report R².

title: Gradient-boosted classifier for 'p has a solution with C ≤ 10' and inspect feature importances
connection: Train a classifier on arithmetic features of p to predict whether a small-C certificate exists; if accuracy is high, the features used ARE a partial identity; if accuracy ≈ base rate, small-C solvability is 'random' w.r.t. all tested features.
why: Cheap, directly reveals structure or its absence in the bounded-C regime (the covering regime).
first_step: Features: p mod 840·k, Legendre symbols of primes ≤ 50, ω and smallest factors of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10; target: exists C ≤ 10 with a winning divisor. Train/test on p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Transformer trained on (p → first solution) to test for learnable 'algorithm'
connection: Train a small transformer on digit sequences p ↦ (x,y,z) for p ≤ 10⁶; test extrapolation to larger p. Charton-style experiments show some arithmetic tasks (GCD, modular arithmetic) are learnable with interpretable circuits.
why: If a model generalises beyond training range, mechanistic interpretability might extract an algorithm; if it cannot, that's weak evidence of no simple algorithm.
first_step: Replicate Charton's GCD-transformer setup with ES targets; measure out-of-range accuracy.
refs: Charton, 'Learning the greatest common divisor', arXiv:2308.15594 (ICLR 2024)

title: Learned certificates: train a model to output C given p, verify by exact arithmetic (AlphaProof-style)
connection: The solution search is 'find C'; a learned prior on C (given features of p) could shrink the search and, more importantly, expose which C-values are 'predictable'.
why: A predictable C-function would be an identity candidate; non-predictability calibrates against covering-type proofs.
first_step: Train a regressor from p-features to log C_min(p); compare against baseline (median); inspect residuals vs p mod 840.

title: Hidden-shift/period structure in the e-slice subset-product sets
connection: The set S_N(e) = {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N} is a 'sumset' in log coordinates; Freiman/Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers structure theorems describe sets with small doubling, and the group-theoretic Kneser theorem gives |S + S| bounds. ES needs −1 ∈ S for some e.
why: Additive-combinatorics structure of S_N could show S_N(e) is 'almost a subgroup' for many e — then membership of −1 is a character-sum question.
first_step: Compute |S_N(e)| and |S·S| relative to e for p ≤ 10⁵ and all admissible e ≤ 4p; look for e where S is a near-subgroup.

title: Complexity-theoretic: is 'ES certificate search' in a class with natural proofs of totality (TFNP subclasses)?
connection: ES says the search problem 'given p, find (x,y,z)' is total. TFNP classes (PPA, PPP, PLS) each correspond to a combinatorial existence principle (parity, pigeonhole, local search). Which principle, if any, would ES's totality be an instance of?
why: PPA-totality = parity argument (e.g. Chevalley–Warning, Smith's theorem), PPP = pigeonhole (Minkowski). If ES is placed in PPA, a parity proof is the target; the campaign has parity-type observations (T1 is a sign) but no parity *proof*.
first_step: Try to express ES as 'a graph with an odd-degree vertex has another' (PPA): build a graph on near-solutions where degrees are determined locally; see if one known odd-degree vertex (e.g. the trivial 'degenerate' solution 4/n = 1/n + 1/n + 2/n?) forces another.

title: Chevalley–Warning / Ax–Katz over ℤ/p: count solutions of 4xyz ≡ n(xy+yz+zx) mod primes to force integer ones
connection: Chevalley–Warning gives p | #solutions mod p of low-degree systems in many variables; the ES equation mod a prime q ≠ p has q² + O(q) points. Can a divisibility invariant on the *integer* solution count (like Markoff's orbit sizes ≡ 0 mod p) be derived?
why: Chen's Markoff proof used an orbit-size divisibility; an analogue 'f(n) ≡ something mod m' with a nonzero RHS would be a parity-type proof of f(n) ≥ 1.
first_step: Compute f(n) mod 2,3,4,6 for n ≤ 10⁵ and check for any forced congruence (e.g. is f(p) always odd for p ≡ 1 mod 24?). Note symmetry: solutions come in permutation orbits, so count orbits.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz for the ES polynomial on a product set
connection: Alon's CN: a polynomial of degree Σ d_i with nonzero coefficient on Π x_i^{d_i} has a non-root on any product set S_1×S_2×S_3 with |S_i| > d_i. ES wants a *root* of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) in a product set — the dual question, but CN-type 'non-vanishing then counting' arguments (e.g. for Cauchy–Davenport) sometimes yield existence of roots of auxiliary polynomials.
why: Listed in the repo's deep-lane catalogue; the free-lane twist: apply CN to an auxiliary polynomial whose non-vanishing implies an ES root (e.g. Π over candidate (x,y) of (something)).
first_step: Try: fix n, consider F(x,y) = Π_{z ∈ Z}(4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx)) over a set Z; CN gives a non-root of F in product sets, i.e. (x,y) such that no z ∈ Z works — the wrong direction. Try instead the polynomial method over F_q with q | some 4Cp+1.

title: Proof-assistant mining: formalise the Type I/II divisor equivalence in Lean/mathlib
connection: mathlib has Egyptian fraction basics? (check: `Nat.Egyptian`? probably not). Formalising the reduction ES(p) ⟺ divisor condition would be a modest contribution and forces every hidden assumption into the open.
why: Formalisation has repeatedly exposed gaps and suggested generalisations; also a public Lean statement attracts collaborators.
first_step: Search mathlib for 'egyptian' and 'unit fraction'; search GitHub for 'Erdős–Straus Lean'; draft the statement `∀ p, Prime p → p % 4 = 1 → (∃ x y z, 4*x*y*z = p*(x*y+y*z+z*x)) ↔ ∃ c d f, ...`.

title: Mine the Lean 'Erdős problems' formalisation project for ES-adjacent lemmas
connection: Erdős problems site + Lean formalisation efforts (e.g. Erdős #306 nearly formalised). ES is Erdős problem #… (check the erdosproblems.com number) — see what lemma infrastructure exists for unit-fraction problems there.
why: Infrastructure reuse; cheap.
first_step: Visit https://www.erdosproblems.com and search 'Straus'; check the associated GitHub for Lean files.

title: Reverse-engineer Salez's 10¹⁷ verification code for implicit structure (which identity family covers which prime)
connection: Salez's verification used a specific set of identities/searches; the *distribution of which family fired first* across primes up to 10¹⁷ is data nobody has analysed for structure.
why: A 'which rule saved this prime' census is a cheap large-scale pattern-discovery dataset.
first_step: Locate Salez's paper/code (arXiv 1406.6307 'The Erdős–Straus conjecture: new modular equations and checking up to N=10^17'); re-run the family census for p ≤ 10⁹ and tabulate first-firing family vs p mod 840.

title: Gröbner basis / elimination for the system {Type I condition, Type II condition} as polynomial equations with p symbolic
connection: The Type I/II parametrisations are polynomial identities in (c,d,f,p). Elimination ideals over ℤ[p] could expose hidden relations between simultaneous Type I and Type II solutions of the same p.
why: Relations between the two types (e.g. a Type I solution implies a Type II for a related prime) would be a new 'persistence' tool.
first_step: In Singular/Macaulay2, set up the ideal generated by 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) with x = pA, etc., and compute elimination ideals; look for any surprise generator.

title: Knuth–Bendix / term rewriting view of the 'Egyptian fraction identities' and confluence
connection: The family of identities (e.g. 1/n = 1/(n+1) + 1/(n(n+1))) forms a rewriting system on multisets of unit fractions; ES asks whether 4/n rewrites to a 3-element multiset. Confluence/termination theory could classify reachable lengths.
why: Formal rewriting makes 'what can be derived from splitting identities' a decidable question in restricted cases; the known tiny families (Bleicher–Erdős) would fit.
first_step: Define rewriting rules: split 1/a → 1/(a+1) + 1/(a(a+1)), merge 1/a + 1/b → 1/c when possible; compute reachable 3-term representations from the greedy 4-term one for n ≤ 1000.

title: Ramsey-type unavoidable patterns: among any K consecutive primes ≡ 1 mod 24, must one have a solution with C ≤ 2?
connection: Even if not every prime has a small-C solution, maybe 'small-C solvability' has bounded gaps along primes (van der Waerden-ish). Not ES itself but a sub-statement with a combinatorial flavour.
why: Bounded-gap statements can be proved by covering + pigeonhole; data shows which K is plausible.
first_step: Compute the longest run of consecutive primes ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁸ with no C ≤ 2 (resp. ≤ 5, ≤ 10) solution.

title: Streaming/sketching: minimal information about p needed to construct a solution
connection: Communication-complexity framing: Alice knows p mod M, Bob knows ⌊p/M⌋; how much communication is needed to agree on an ES solution? If O(1) bits suffice for some M, that's a covering system; if Θ(log p), solutions are 'global'.
why: A clean quantitative version of 'ES is not local' (Mordell–Schinzel says polynomial-local fails; this asks for any protocol).
first_step: Empirically: for M = 840, compute for each residue class r the size of the smallest 'dictionary' of solution templates (c,d) needed to cover all primes ≡ r up to 10⁶; growth with the range.

title: Hash-function / pseudorandomness: treat (p ↦ prime factorisation of 4Cp+1) as a PRG and ES as 'PRG never outputs the all-miss pattern'
connection: Cryptographic pseudorandomness would *predict* P(miss) ≈ exp(−c log²p) and that misses happen for some p; ES asserts that they never happen — i.e. the map is detectably non-pseudorandom in the lower tail.
why: Forces a clear statement: either ES's 'never' is a coincidence of the small-count regime (and there IS a counterexample), or there is a structural correlation across C. The question 'which' is the campaign's central dilemma; the crypto framing suggests testing *higher-order correlations* across C.
first_step: Measure pairwise and triple correlations between the events 'C wins' and 'C′ wins' for p ≤ 10⁷; compare to independent model.

title: LLL on the 3-variable ES equation directly: find small solutions to 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) = 0 via Coppersmith bivariate
connection: After fixing x (≈ n/4 + small), the equation in (y,z) is a bivariate integer polynomial of bidegree (1,1): (4x − n)yz − nx(y+z) = 0 ⇒ ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = n²x². So solutions are divisor pairs of n²x² in classes — Coppersmith's bivariate method finds small roots.
why: The factorisation ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = n²x² is the classical two-term reduction; the 'small root' regime y,z ≤ n^{1+ε} may be exactly where solutions live. Quantify.
first_step: Check numerically: for p ≤ 10⁶, what is min over solutions of max(y,z)/p? Does a solution with max ≤ p^{3/2} always exist? (Relates to known bounds on denominators.)

title: Smallest-solution growth: is min_{solutions} max(x,y,z) ≤ p^{1+o(1)}?
connection: Bounds on the size of the smallest solution are a different pointwise statement than existence; the exponent governs which algorithmic approaches (Coppersmith bivariate: roots up to N^{1/3}…) could be made *provably* complete.
why: If the smallest solution has max coordinate ≈ p^{3/2} typically, then no 'small roots' method is complete; if ≈ p log p, there's hope for a lattice-based constructive proof.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁷ the smallest max-coordinate solution and fit the growth exponent; check repo for existing data (git grep -i 'smallest solution\|max(x,y,z)').

title: Word problem in SL₂(ℤ): ES as membership of a specific matrix in a product of three 'elementary' cosets
connection: Repo mentions SL₂ words. Membership-in-product-set problems in SL₂(ℤ) are decidable (automaticity of SL₂) and have automaton-theoretic structure; the 'length ≤ 3' condition of ES₅ is a bounded word length.
why: Automata for SL₂(ℤ) (via the free product ℤ/4 * ℤ/6) give a regular-language description of 'length ≤ 3 words'; the question becomes whether a regular language intersects a p-dependent set, which is sometimes handled by Büchi-type decidability over (ℕ, +, V_k).
first_step: Write the ES₅ word form as an explicit matrix product with entries depending on p; check whether the condition is 'matrix M_p is in L' for a regular L in the generator alphabet.

title: Constraint-propagation / arc-consistency on the (c,d,f) space to prove 'no solution' is contradictory
connection: CSP solvers find contradictions by propagating constraints; for a *symbolic* p (represented by its residues mod many small moduli), propagation might derive that 'no solution for any C ≤ K' contradicts p being prime ≡ 1 mod 24 for some K.
why: This is the covering-system search re-done with a general-purpose propagator that can also use quadratic-residuosity constraints (not just congruences) — which Mordell–Schinzel does not forbid.
first_step: Encode: p ≡ r mod 840; for each C ≤ K, all divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C forbidden ⟹ constraints on Legendre symbols (−C/q) for q | 4Cp+1; propagate; look for contradiction with K ≤ 20.

title: Pseudo-Boolean / ILP relaxation: lower bound f(p) via LP duality on the e-slice counting polytope
connection: Write f(p) = Σ over e-slices of #{(a,b)}; an LP relaxation with constraints from divisor-sum identities (Σ_e over slices of total divisor counts = known) might give a dual certificate f(p) ≥ 1 if the identities are strong enough.
why: LP duality turns 'existence' into 'an explicit positive combination of known identities exceeds 0' — a proof template that is mechanically checkable.
first_step: Set up for p = 1009 (small): variables = indicator of each (e, a, b) candidate; constraints = all linear identities the campaign knows (divisor totals per e, M_BM-type sums); solve the LP; see whether the LP bound is > 0.

title: Sum-of-squares (Positivstellensatz) certificate that the ES count is positive for a symbolic p in a residue class
connection: Positivstellensatz gives algebraic certificates of positivity of polynomials on semialgebraic sets; the ES count isn't polynomial in p, but a surrogate (e.g. a weighted divisor sum with explicit character expansion) could be expressed via finite sums over residues of p mod M.
why: SOS has proved inequalities in combinatorics (flag algebras) that were beyond human reach; the challenge is finding a finite algebraic surrogate.
first_step: Fix M = 840; express Σ_{C ≤ K} Σ_{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)} 1 ≥ (Σ over C of a quadratic-character sum in p mod stuff) and see if any lower bound depends only on p mod M.

title: Boolean function analysis: Fourier spectrum of the indicator 'C wins for p' as a function of p mod 4C·something
connection: For fixed C, whether 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C depends on p via the factorisation of 4Cp+1; its Fourier spectrum over p mod M (M a multiple of 4C) measures 'junta-ness'.
why: A low-degree Fourier concentration for all C would be a covering-ish structure; spectrum spread across high frequencies says the event is genuinely 'global'.
first_step: Compute, for C ≤ 20 and M = lcm(4C, 840), the Fourier spectrum (over ℤ/M) of E_p[win_C(p) | p ≡ r mod M] for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Property testing: can one certify ES(p) with o(log p) queries to an oracle for the factorisation of 4Cp+1?
connection: Query complexity of the existence problem given a factorisation oracle: how many C must be queried in the worst case (empirically) before a winner is found? The query sequence design (adaptive vs non-adaptive) is the algorithmic skeleton of a proof.
why: Worst-case query counts over p ≤ 10⁸ calibrate the 'depth' of a proof (K queries ⇒ a K-case argument).
first_step: Record C_min(p) distribution (non-adaptive) and design an adaptive rule (choose next C based on factorisation of previous 4Cp+1); measure the max number of queries for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Automated theorem proving on the 'two-term' lemma with a free parameter: Vampire/E on the divisor form
connection: First-order provers can sometimes prove number-theoretic lemmas given axioms about divisibility; the lemma 'if p ≡ 1 mod 24 and p < 2^k then ∃C ≤ K ...' is a bounded statement they might handle for small k.
why: Low chance, but the prover's search traces for small k might reveal which lemmas are reused — a proof-skeleton extraction.
first_step: Encode the divisor form in TPTP with Peano arithmetic axioms + bounded quantifiers; try Vampire for k ≤ 8.

title: Zero-knowledge-style 'succinct witness' for ES(p): what is the shortest certificate as a function of p?
connection: A solution (x,y,z) is a 3·log p-bit witness; a (C, divisor) is 2·log p bits; the ES₅ CF form is ~log p + small. The minimal witness length (information-theoretically) across p is a 'compressibility of the certificate'.
why: If a witness of O(log log p) extra bits beyond p exists for every p (i.e. 'which of polylog many templates'), ES is 'almost covered' by a polylog-size list — a different proof shape than existing ones.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁷, the minimal index of a winning C in the ordering by C; its log is the witness length; compare growth with log log p.

title: Union-find / disjoint-set structure of 'solution sharing' between different primes
connection: Two primes share a template if the same (c,d) with the forced f gives solutions for both. Build the graph on primes ≤ X with edges = shared template; connected components and their growth describe how 'global' the solution structure is.
why: Giant-component formation would indicate a Markoff-like 'strong approximation' phenomenon; many tiny components would indicate per-prime independence.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, list templates (c,d) of all solutions, build the bipartite prime–template graph, compute component structure.

title: Monte-Carlo tree search over 'proof strategies' for small residue classes (AlphaZero for covering systems)
connection: The search for a covering system of identities is itself a game tree; MCTS/RL has found covering-type constructions in other settings (e.g. Wagner's RL for combinatorial counterexamples). Target: maximal density of primes ≡ 1 mod 840 coverable by degree-≤2 identities with moduli ≤ M.
why: Not a proof, but establishes the best achievable 'partial cover' and whether the uncovered set has structure (squares + ?).
first_step: Reproduce the known cover (Mordell + Salez families) as a baseline; implement the RL search over identity templates; report uncovered density vs M.
refs: Wagner, 'Constructions in combinatorics via neural networks' (2021)

title: Quantum annealing formulation of ES as QUBO — purely to inspect the energy landscape
connection: Encode the bit-blasted equation as a QUBO; the spectrum of the Ising Hamiltonian (gap between ground state and first excited) across p measures 'hardness'; a gap that scales mildly suggests structure.
why: Cheap curiosity test; may reveal p-dependence of the landscape.
first_step: Build QUBO for p ≤ 200 via standard multiplication gadgets; exact-diagonalise small instances; plot gap vs p.

title: Compressed sensing / sparse recovery: f(p) as a sparse combination of character sums
connection: Express f(p) (or its Type I part) as Σ_χ c_χ χ(p) over characters of various moduli (it's not periodic, but truncated versions are); sparse recovery finds the dominant characters. Dominant terms = the identities that matter most.
why: Quantifies 'how periodic is f(p)' beyond Mordell's mod 840; a sparse spectrum would suggest a near-covering.
first_step: Fit f(p) − A log²p on p ≤ 10⁷ against characters mod M ≤ 10⁴ with LASSO; list top characters.

title: Model-checking a finite abstraction: ES for p 'with all small primes' residues fixed' as a finite transition system
connection: Abstract p by its residues mod all primes ≤ B and by its Legendre symbols; a finite-state system over these abstractions can be model-checked for the property 'some C ≤ K yields a divisor in class'. Counterexample traces are candidate hard residue profiles.
why: Finds the exact abstract profile of a potential counterexample; such profiles could then be hunted at 10¹⁸ (adversarial search guidance).
first_step: Enumerate profiles of p mod 840 and Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 31; for each profile, compute the empirical fraction of primes with C_min ≤ 10; find worst profiles.

title: Error-correcting codes: solution sets as codewords, and ES as 'minimum distance ≥ 1 from the zero word'
connection: Define for each p the binary vector v_p ∈ {0,1}^K with v_p[C] = 1 if C wins. ES(p) for C ≤ K ⟺ v_p ≠ 0. The set {v_p} is a 'code'; its minimum weight (over p) and its dual structure may reveal linear constraints among the C's.
why: Linear constraints among win-events (over F₂) would be exactly the parity invariants that could force a win.
first_step: Compute v_p for K = 64 and p ≤ 10⁶; compute the F₂-rank of the matrix and look for low-weight dual codewords (parity checks).

title: Database cross-reference: OEIS sequences around f(n), C_min, and Egyptian-fraction lengths
connection: OEIS has A073101 (number of solutions of 4/n), A192787, etc. Looking at the 'sequences that reference these' and their formulas/comments may reveal a connection the campaign missed.
why: Cheap and occasionally very fruitful.
first_step: Fetch OEIS A073101, A192787, A192788, A192789 and all sequences citing 'Erdős–Straus'; read comments and formulas; list any with unexpected cross-references (e.g. to class numbers, Bernoulli, Markoff).

title: Grover-style amplitude amplification is irrelevant, but the quantum query lower bound technique (adversary method) applies to classical 'how many C must be tried'
connection: Adversary bounds give lower bounds on queries needed to find a winning C against a worst-case p; translated classically: any proof that tries C in a fixed order needs ≥ max C_min(p) cases.
why: Makes precise that a 'list of templates' proof must have unbounded length — reinforcing Mordell–Schinzel from an algorithmic angle, but also showing adaptive proofs are not bound by it.
first_step: Just note it; verify unboundedness of C_min(p) numerically (if C_min were bounded a finite cover would exist — contradiction with Mordell–Schinzel only for polynomial covers; so unbounded C_min is a separate empirical question!). Compute max C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁸.

title: Is C_min(p) actually bounded? (sanity question separating covering from identities)
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids *polynomial* identities on square classes but does not forbid 'for every prime p ≡ 1 mod 24 some C ≤ 10⁶ works'. If C_min is empirically bounded (e.g. ≤ 1000 up to 10¹⁸) that is a striking structural fact; if it grows like log p, there is no finite cover at all.
why: This is the single most basic calibration of the 'covering' approach and the question is sharp and cheap.
first_step: git grep -il 'C_min\|bounded C\|smallest C' -- '*.md'; if absent, compute max_{p ≤ 10⁸} C_min(p) with C in Type II form and in e-slice form.

title: Lattice attack on 'ES with x fixed to the greedy choice': when does greedy-first-term lead to a two-term remainder?
connection: The Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy picks x = ⌈n/4⌉; the remainder (4x−n)/(nx) with 4x − n ∈ {1,2,3} is a two-term sum iff a divisor condition on nx holds. For 4x − n = 1: 1/(nx) is one unit fraction, so greedy gives 2 terms? No: n ≡ 3 mod 4 case gives 1/(nx) — that's the easy class. For n ≡ 1 mod 4, 4x − n = 3 and 3/(nx) must split into two unit fractions.
why: The hard class p ≡ 1 mod 4 is exactly 'is 3/(p·⌈p/4⌉) a sum of two unit fractions, or else choose a non-greedy x'; the two-term criterion for 3/m is classical (3/m = 1/a + 1/b iff m has a divisor pattern mod 3). Making the 'non-greedy x' choice explicit is the whole game and the lattice view (x free, divisor of p²x² in class) is clean.
first_step: Tabulate for p ≤ 10⁶ the smallest x ≥ ⌈p/4⌉ such that (4x−p)/(px) is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study x − ⌈p/4⌉ distribution (is it O(log p)? polylog?).

title: Bit-level pattern mining on winning C in binary (are winning C's 'smooth'? 'prime'? 'powers of 2'?)
connection: The multiplicative structure of winning C matters (4C is the modulus); test whether winning C are biased toward smooth numbers, primes, or specific residue classes mod 3, 5, 7.
why: A bias (e.g. winning C is often a multiple of 3 for p ≡ 1 mod 3) is a candidate identity direction; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ collect all winning C ≤ 1000; compare their distribution of ω(C), smoothness, C mod 12 against the uniform baseline.

title: De Bruijn / universal cycle: does a single 'universal' residue sequence of C's cover all primes up to X with O(log X) entries?
connection: Hitting-set problem: find the smallest set S of C's such that every prime p ≤ X has a winner in S. Its growth |S(X)| in X (constant? log X? X^ε?) is the 'covering dimension' of ES.
why: If |S(X)| = O(log X) with a nice structure (e.g. S = {1,2,3,6,...} products of small primes), a 'nested cover' proof shape emerges.
first_step: Greedy set-cover on the prime–C incidence matrix for p ≤ 10⁷, C ≤ 10⁴; report |S| vs X.

title: Tropical geometry of the ES surface: the tropical variety of 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) and lattice points on its 'tentacles'
connection: Tropicalising the cubic surface gives a piecewise-linear complex whose lattice points approximate valuations of solutions; the 'size' of solutions (val_q(x), …) lives on the tropical surface.
why: Tropical methods count/locate solutions by valuations — maybe they explain the preferred shape (one coordinate ≈ p, others ≈ p²/…).
first_step: Compute the tropical hypersurface of the Newton polytope of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) (with n's valuation as a parameter) and plot where known solutions' (log x, log y, log z) fall.

title: Reed–Solomon-type interpolation: can the map p ↦ (x,y,z) be interpolated by a low-degree polynomial over a finite field F_q?
connection: Over F_q (q a prime of size ~ range), the 'first solution' map restricted to primes is a function; its degree as a polynomial over F_q (via interpolation) compared to the number of points measures 'algebraicity'.
why: If the map had degree far below the number of points for structured subsets (e.g. primes in a fixed class mod M), those subsets are covered by an algebraic rule — a new identity family.
first_step: Take primes ≡ 1 mod 840 up to 10⁵, interpolate C_min(p) mod q as a polynomial in p mod q, check the degree vs number of points; expect full degree (no structure) — a negative result calibrates B1.

title: Verification scale-up as a lead generator: GPU search for primes with anomalously small f(p)
connection: Adversarial search beyond 10¹⁸ for 'hardest primes' (minimum f(p)/log²p) over structured families (p with many small QNRs, p = m² + small); the hardest ones are the stress tests for any candidate mechanism.
why: Repo has adversarial data; extending it with GPU and a better hardness oracle (Legendre-symbol profiles) is cheap and gives a test suite for proposed proofs.
first_step: Define a hardness proxy from Legendre symbols (p/q) for q ≤ 50 (minimising predicted small-C wins); sample 10⁶ primes near 10²⁰ with worst proxy; count solutions on C ≤ 10⁴.

title: Croot's proof of Erdős–Graham (unit fractions with denominators in one colour class): the 'smooth numbers + exponential sums' method
connection: Croot (Annals 2003) shows any finite colouring of integers has a monochromatic set with Σ 1/n = 1; the proof uses smooth numbers in an interval and a Fourier/exponential-sum count of subset sums. ES is a 3-term, fixed-numerator version with no colouring freedom.
why: Croot's technology is the most powerful known for 'exact unit-fraction sum' problems; understanding exactly which freedom it needs (many terms, smooth denominators) sharpens what 3-term ES lacks — and whether a 'many-term then merge' route exists (merge identities 1/a + 1/b = 1/c when a+b | ab).
first_step: Read Croot 2003 §2; list the three places where the number of terms is used; check whether any merge lemma (k terms → 3 terms when denominators share structure) can be bolted on; search 'merging unit fractions into three'.
refs: Croot, 'On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions', Ann. Math. 157 (2003)

title: Bloom's density proof of Erdős–Graham (2021) and its Lean formalisation: Fourier-analytic unit fraction counting
connection: Bloom proves every set of positive upper density contains a finite subset with Σ 1/n = 1; formalised in Lean (Bloom–Mehta). The Fourier method counts solutions of Σ 1/n_i = 1 among many candidates.
why: The formalised infrastructure (unit-fraction sums, Fourier counting) is reusable; and Bloom's 'local' lemma (sum = 1 using denominators in a short interval of smooth numbers) may give 'ES over short intervals' statements (e.g. every x ∈ [N, 2N] has 4/x as a sum of ≤ k unit fractions from a prescribed set).
first_step: Read Bloom 2021 Thm 3 and the Lean repository 'unit-fractions'; identify what the key counting proposition gives for *fixed* numerator 4 and 3 terms (probably nothing: it needs many terms); record exactly why.
refs: Bloom, 'On a density conjecture about unit fractions', arXiv:2112.03726

title: Sylvester's 1880 sequence and Egyptian fraction 'denominator growth': why 3-term is the hard case
connection: Sylvester's greedy gives 4/n in ≤ 4 terms always; the gap between 4 (easy, greedy) and 3 (open) is the whole conjecture. Historically, similar 'one fewer term' gaps were closed by divisor-structure lemmas (e.g. Nagell's results on 2/n, 3/n).
why: Revisit how the k = 2 and numerator 2, 3 cases were resolved (they are theorems); the proof pattern for 3/n (always ≤ 2 terms? no: 3/n = 2 terms iff n has a divisor ≡ 2 mod 3; else 3 terms) suggests that ES is the first case where the 'iff' divisor criterion is not local — which is exactly Mordell–Schinzel. Document the exact historical sequence of results.
first_step: Search and read: Nagell 1922/23 on a/n = 1/x + 1/y; Mordell's chapter 30; list which cases (numerator a, k terms) are theorems and by what method.

title: Rhind papyrus 2/n table: did the Egyptian scribes' decomposition rules form a covering system?
connection: The 2/n table decomposes 2/n (odd n ≤ 101) into 2–4 unit fractions by patterns depending on n's factors; scholars (Gillings, Abdulaziz) reconstructed the rules. The structure is a historical 'covering by identities' for numerator 2.
why: Recreational/historical lens; the scribes' choice of 'nice' decompositions (small, even denominators) foreshadows the modern preference for Type I/II; cheap read.
first_step: Read Abdulaziz 'On the Egyptian method of decomposing 2/n into unit fractions' (Historia Math 2008) and note whether any rule there generalises to 4/n with 3 terms.

title: Erdős's own heuristic for ES in 'Some unconventional problems in number theory' and his 'Sierpiński 5/n' remark
connection: Erdős (and Sierpiński for 5/n, Schinzel for a/n with n ≥ n₀(a)) framed the conjecture; Schinzel's generalisation 'a/n in 3 unit fractions for n ≥ n₀(a)' is the natural family. Tools that handle ALL a simultaneously may be forced to use structure invisible for a = 4.
why: The a-family (a/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n ≥ n₀(a)) is a 2-parameter problem; results for specific a (Sierpiński 5/n verified far; Palamà, Yamamoto for a ≤ 36?) and their methods are a direct lead library.
first_step: Search 'Schinzel conjecture a/n three unit fractions n_0(a)' and compile the status table for a ≤ 40 (who proved what, by which identities); check whether any a-value was handled by a non-covering argument.

title: Yamamoto's 1965 proof that odd squares have no Type I/II solutions — read the original for *spare* structure
connection: Yamamoto's argument (reciprocity) is T1. Original papers often contain more than the cited theorem (e.g. a characterisation of which n have f_I = 0).
why: If Yamamoto characterised all n with f_I(n) = 0 (not just squares) the campaign's U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, …} might be explained; also his method's 'failure at squares' may be invertible into a 'success at non-squares' condition.
first_step: Obtain Yamamoto, 'On the Diophantine equation 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z', Mem. Fac. Sci. Kyushu Univ. 19 (1965); read all lemmas; compare with the U(n) sporadic list.

title: Rosati 1954 / Bernstein 1962 / Webb 1970 / Vaughan 1970: trace the lineage of exceptional-set bounds for the 'thin' idea that was dropped
connection: The exceptional-set line (Webb, Vaughan, Elsholtz–Tao, Elsholtz–Planitzer) improved E(N) by better sieving; each paper's 'what we could not do' section records the pointwise obstruction in the author's words.
why: Someone in 1970 may have had an idea for pointwise bounds that was abandoned for being 'too hard', not wrong.
first_step: Read Vaughan 1970 Mathematika §4 (final remarks) and Webb 1970 Proc. AMS; note any conditional or partial pointwise statement.
refs: Vaughan, 'On a problem of Erdős, Straus and Schinzel', Mathematika 17 (1970)

title: Elsholtz–Tao §'open questions' list — re-audit which are now answered and which lead to ES
connection: ET 2013 list several open problems (lower bounds on f(n) for all n? distribution of Type I vs II; polynomial identities). A decade later, some may be resolved in papers not yet in the repo.
why: Cheap literature update with precise targets.
first_step: Re-read ET §1.3–1.4 'open problems'; for each, search arXiv 2013–2026 (citations of ET via Semantic Scholar) and note status.

title: Ask Christian Elsholtz / Stefan Planitzer directly what they consider the current frontier
connection: People item: the authors of the almost-all lower bound f(n) ≥ (log n)^{log 6 + o(1)} are the closest active experts; a short email with the campaign's barrier map attached could elicit either a known dead-end or a tip.
why: Human expert input is cheap relative to the search cost; the campaign's FRONTIER.md is a ready-made attachment.
first_step: Draft a 10-line email summarising the single-integer lower tail (FRONTIER §2) and asking (i) is this reduction known, (ii) any route they abandoned; send.
refs: Elsholtz–Planitzer, 'Egyptian fractions and the Erdős–Straus conjecture' (Monatsh. Math 2020?)

title: Post the single-integer lower tail as a MathOverflow question
connection: FRONTIER §2's reduction ('a specific integer tied to p must have a divisor in a class with modulus part of the solution') is a clean, citable question for MO: 'Is there any known theorem giving ≥1 divisor in a tied residue class for every n?'
why: MO has answered 'is there any theorem of shape X' questions well (experts recall obscure results); low cost.
first_step: Write the MO question with the precise statement (4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C for some C), the heuristic count log²p, and the known results (Lenstra upper bound, almost-all results); post under number-theory tag.

title: Pólya–Vinogradov-era people: ask Igor Shparlinski about divisor-restricted modular hyperbola points
connection: Shparlinski has many papers on modular hyperbolas and on divisors in residue classes; the exact ES-shaped question (points on xy ≡ −1 mod e with x,y | N) is in his wheelhouse.
why: People item; cheap; he may know a relevant character-sum bound or a reason it's hopeless.
first_step: Email with the e-slice formulation; ask whether 'hyperbola points with both coordinates dividing a given N' has been studied.

title: Contact Bright and Loughran about an integral-Brauer–Manin *refinement* at the ES fibre
connection: BL showed no BM obstruction; the campaign found the Brauer class dies at the ES fibre k = 0. Ask them whether any finer invariant (descent obstruction, étale-Brauer, or 'integral points on log K3 / cubic surfaces with 3 A₁ singularities') applies to U_n.
why: The surface people know what finer obstructions exist; cheap to ask.
first_step: Email summarising Z52_BANKED 'why the obvious Brauer class dies at k = 0'; ask about étale-Brauer and about Harpaz–Wittenberg fibration method for integral points.

title: Thomas Bloom's unit-fractions Lean library as a base for an 'ES data' formal verification
connection: The Bloom–Mehta Lean project has definitions for unit fraction sums; a formally verified 'ES holds for all n ≤ 10⁶ via these certificates' would be a small but citable deliverable and a test of mathlib infrastructure.
why: Formal verification of computations is now routine; cheap.
first_step: Clone the unit-fractions repo; write a `decide`/`native_decide` based checker for 4/n certificates for n ≤ 10⁴ first.

title: Conference lens: which 2026–27 meetings have unit fractions / Egyptian fractions sessions (Integers, CANT, ELAZ)?
connection: CANT (Combinatorial and Additive Number Theory, NYC), the INTEGERS conference, and ELAZ host unit-fraction talks regularly; abstracts there may contain unpublished partial results.
why: Cheap scan.
first_step: Fetch the abstracts of CANT 2024–2026 and INTEGERS 2025; grep for 'unit fraction', 'Egyptian', 'Straus'.

title: Mordell's chapter 30 'the equation 4/n' — the discarded alternative parametrisations
connection: Mordell lists several families beyond the mod-840 ones and remarks on their limitations; the discarded families may be non-polynomial in disguise.
why: Primary-source check; the campaign cites Mordell via secondary literature.
first_step: Read Mordell ch. 30 fully; transcribe every identity and its residue class; compare with the repo's identity census (git grep -il 'identit' -- 'DISCOVERIES.md').

title: Stewart–Tijdeman / Bleicher: 'Egyptian fractions with denominators in a bounded set of prime factors' (S-unit viewpoint)
connection: Restrict x,y,z to S-units (or to numbers with prime factors from a set S); 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z becomes an S-unit equation xy + yz + zx = (4/n)xyz with finitely many solutions (Evertse). For varying n, the count is tied to S.
why: S-unit theory gives finiteness + effective bounds (Baker); ES wants infinitude across n, but the S-unit lens might explain the preferred shapes of solutions (denominators smooth relative to p).
first_step: Compute the smoothness of (x,y,z)/p-part for the first solution of each p ≤ 10⁶; are the non-p parts typically (log p)-smooth? If so, the S-unit equation over a fixed S ∪ {p} is the right finite problem per p.

title: Geometry of numbers: Minkowski's theorem on the 'Type II' lattice to force a divisor pair
connection: Type II: ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd.
